Stepwise linear-regression feature selection by AIC

Source: R/fs_stepwise.R
fs_stepwise.Rd

Finds the subset of columns that AIC keeps in a linear model. Uses MASS::stepAIC() to add or drop one term at a time from a linear regression of target on all other columns of data, stopping when no single move lowers AIC. Requires the suggested package 'MASS'.

Usage

fs_stepwise(
  data,
  target,
  direction = c("both", "backward", "forward"),
  verbose = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

data

A data.frame (or data.table) with at least two columns, the numeric target and at least one candidate predictor, with unique, non-empty column names and no infinite values. Every column other than target is offered to the search. For backward and both-direction searches, the complete rows must outnumber the coefficients of the full model.

target

Single string naming the numeric target column of data. Unquoted symbols and column indices are not accepted. Non-syntactic names work, because they are backticked in the formula.

direction

Direction of the search: "both" (the default), "backward", or "forward".

verbose

Logical. If TRUE, print progress messages and the stepAIC() trace. Default FALSE.

...

Further arguments passed to MASS::stepAIC(), for example k (k = log(nrow(data)) gives BIC), steps, or scope (which then replaces the default scope). trace is controlled by verbose, and a trace supplied here is dropped with a warning. See Details for what else ... absorbs.

Value

An object of class fs_result with:

selected

Character vector of the selected predictor terms, without the intercept.

scores

Named numeric vector with one entry per selected term, keyed like selected: the absolute t statistic of the term's coefficient or, for a term with several coefficients (a factor, an interaction), the largest |t| among them (NA when all are aliased). The per-coefficient values (for example grpb and grpc for the term grp) are in details$coefficient_scores. These statistics are computed after selection on the same data, so they are optimistically biased and not valid for inference.

method

"stepwise".

task

"regression"; fs_stepwise() fits linear models only.

model

The lm chosen by stepAIC(). It carries a copy of the complete-case data in a private environment (see Details).

details

A list with final_model (the same lm), coefficients (the summary() coefficient matrix, biased like scores), coefficient_scores (named |t| per non-intercept coefficient), selected_terms (the same labels as selected), direction (the search direction used), n_features (the number of candidate predictors, ncol(data) - 1), and dropped_na_rows (the number of rows removed for missing values, 0L when none were).

call

The matched call.

Details

This is the cheapest wrapper method in featR and the easiest to read: the result is an ordinary lm that the usual generics work on. The search is greedy, so it can walk past the AIC-best subset, and unstable, so small changes in the data can change the retained set.

The reported scores (absolute t statistics) and the p-values in details$coefficients are computed on the same data that drove the search. They are optimistically biased (the selective-inference problem) and are not valid for formal inference; use them only as a rough ordering of the retained terms.

Only linear regression is supported: the target must be numeric, and every other column of data is a candidate predictor. direction = "backward" starts from the full model; "forward" starts from the intercept-only model with the full model as the upper scope; "both" starts from the full model with the same scope, so terms can be added back. There is no seed argument: stepAIC() is deterministic, so the same call on the same data returns the same model, and the RNG is never touched.

Rows with a missing value in any column are dropped, with a warning, before the search, because stepAIC() cannot compare models fitted on different rows. Infinite values are an error.

Backward and both-direction searches start from the full model, which must leave residual degrees of freedom. With as many coefficients (intercept and factor dummies included) as complete rows, the full model fits perfectly, its AIC is -Inf, and the call stops with an error giving the counts. A forward search may have more candidate predictors than rows; it warns if the model it ends on has no residual degrees of freedom, since that perfect fit makes the selection meaningless. A factor or character predictor with fewer than two observed levels (after incomplete rows are dropped) is an error, as is a factor dummy name that collides with another column or the target (factor g with level b next to a column gb).

The models reach their data through a private environment attached to the model formula, so predict(), summary(), anova(), add1(), drop1() and similar generics work on the returned model. Nothing is assigned to the global environment or written to disk. That environment holds a copy of the complete-case data and is kept alive by the returned model, so the returned object is at least as large as that copy. Plain update(model) fails with an object-not-found error, because update() re-evaluates the stored call in the caller's environment, where the private data is not visible. Pass the data explicitly instead: update(model, . ~ . - x, data = my_data).

Non-syntactic column names are backticked in the formula and reported without the backticks, so selected matches names(data).

... is forwarded to MASS::stepAIC() unchanged, so it also swallows arguments this function does not have. The removed arguments seed and return_models are passed through and ignored rather than rejected: a call written for the older interface still runs, without the effect it asked for. Check your argument names against the list below.

See also

The Wrapper methods guide, which runs this function on a worked example.

Examples

if (requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)) {
  res <- fs_stepwise(mtcars, target = "mpg", direction = "both")
  print(res$selected)
  # |t| of the retained terms: a rough ordering, not valid inference
  print(res$scores)

  # the returned model is an ordinary lm, but update() needs 'data'
  refit <- stats::update(res$model, . ~ . - wt, data = mtcars)
  print(stats::formula(refit))
}
#> [1] "wt"   "qsec" "am"  
#>       wt     qsec       am 
#> 5.506882 4.246676 2.080819 
#> mpg ~ qsec + am
#> <environment: 0x55842f31bbb8>
